title: I’m creating a game using Midjourney for the illustrations. Which style is least likely to put people off?
author: Blasckout
selftext:
Some of the images in my game were generated using Midjourney. As well as the general criticism of AI, people also told me (probably quite rightly) that the artwork on the page looked too much like AI slop.  
  
Although I can’t do without AI-generated art, the truth is that the anime style still visible on the Steam page might really rub people up the wrong way, especially those who are used to seeing AI-generated art.

Obviously, I’m not trying to mislead people into thinking this is art created by humans; I just want to do my best within the field of AI-generated art.  
  
So I’ve created the same promotional video in two new styles that I think work better and feel less like AI slop (graphic novel versus pixel art), and I’ve run an A/B test on Reddit: two identical adverts that differed only in their images.  
  
Unfortunately, with a CTR of around 2.25 per cent for both adverts, the result was a statistical tie.

  
So I’m still unable to resolve this dilemma and would appreciate your help with your opinion.  
  
The game’s Steam page (still featuring a more typical, AI-generated style for now): 

[Delphi on Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4751280/Delphi/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=page_launch&utm_content=reddit_en_abstyle)  
  
  
Thanks!

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body: They both look like typical Midjourney style images to me. The only way you can avoid putting people off is by making your art assets not look like AI.

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: Thanks for your reply! Any suggestions on how to achieve this in Midjourney or elsewhere?

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: Any recommendations? I think Midjourney produces a very aesthetically pleasing result, but perhaps that’s what makes it look so much like AI.

comments.author: Obi_1_K3n0b1
comments.body:
PC game consumers are very picky about AI generated art. If I were you, I would take the images you have right now, and redraw them yourself in a minimalist art style (maybe 3-8 minutes per picture, depending on size.) 

That’s probably not what you want to hear, but it is extremely common for people to completely skip over and ignore games for using AI art, and therefore necessary you make original assets to give your game a chance.

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: Thank you for your honesty! When I decided to make the game this way, I didn’t realise there would be so much opposition to the use of AI. But if I wanted to use cards with images, there would be hundreds of them. I’d have to rethink the whole game or simplify it considerably. That’s why I was trying to create a good style whilst accepting the drawbacks of using AI.

replies.author: LinkesAuge
replies.body:
Do not listen to him. There is no way that you will get any decent results with just 3-8 minutes per picture even if you were the most talented artist out there and underwhelming art is just as bad as obvious AI art.

There are a million ways to "un-AI" your images/styles. The core part is to establish your own prompting system and workflow and obviously not to just use a super generic prompt. Mix and match styles/directions in your baseline, try to give it your own twist and based on these establish a style guideline as well as references that can be consistently followed. That's usually the biggest "tell" for AI, not that people would spot single images as "AI" but that there is a lack of consistency.  
There is for example nothing stopping you from telling an image model to create a "minimalist" look at first and then further shape that in the next steps of your workflow.  
That's how you can get very "unique" looks, don't try to get everything right in one try/output.

You can also strengthen your own style by using procedural adjustments for your AI outputs, ie there are plenty of ways to "postprocess" things to bring them visually closer together and yes that can also include doing things per hand afterwards, that's of course not forbidden but you need to pick your battles.

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: Thanks for your reply! It’s clear I need to keep working on it. I think I was struggling to achieve consistency in Midjourney. That’s why I thought that perhaps the more defined pixel art style would be less likely to stray from that consistency and might look better. It’s the first time I’ve worked with AI art and I was finding it hard to spot the flaws you’ve pointed out. Thanks again!

replies.author: LinkesAuge
replies.body:
Look into ComfyUI and workflows in there. I know it can be daunting but it's one of the best tools to create an actual "pipeline" and make things your own and more importantly let's you also engage with a wider range of image models (and loras) and also test / explore at scale.  
But even outside of that and while using "just" Midjourney, don't just randomly try prompts.  
You have AI agents at your fingertips. They are great at creating structure and tools to get organized. Ask them to create consistent prompt structures, to make suggestions for art styles/direction, let them improve your prompts, track what you generated, what works or doesn't work, be systematic and figure out what brings you good results.

PS: Pixel art has quite a range of "styles" too and it is also a very oversaturated design direction so it can have the opposite effect.   
Besides that Midjourney is a very "opinionated" and very "artistic" image model to begin with which is imo why I don't consider it a good choice for use cases like this as you always inherit its strong opinions. That helps you to get pretty looking results quickly but it makes it harder to steer into your own direction (not impossible but keep that in mind).

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body:
I tried out ComfyUI with Flux models and some recommended workflows, but at first I thought the results looked a bit rough around the edges. Perhaps it was because I was initially going for a more anime-style look. I’ll keep trying out alternatives and following your advice, and I’ll be more systematic with the generation process.

Yes, I’ve noticed that even with pixel art, Midjourney still applies its own stylisation and it’s difficult to get away from that.

Thank you for all your help!

replies.author: MunchyCerealGuy
replies.body: Yeah, comfyui is typically used by professionals who expect to touch things up manually using manually maneuvered apps like photoshop, aseprite, adobe illustrator. etc. I was at the game developers conference (GDC) this year where Comfy had a booth and one of the guys there had hundreds of thousands of followers on instagram for making videos of transformations made entirely with comfy where every video takes hours to make

replies.author: Obi_1_K3n0b1
replies.body: Thats a fair point. Although I will say, I can get decent to good results doing 3-8 minutes per large sprite/background, but obviously I should’ve taken into consideration they might not be able to.

comments.author: ImaginaryProgram142
comments.body: There are also many of us who will accept AI so long as the assets are consistent, and adequate effort has been put into the finished product.

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: Thanks for your reply! Perhaps it wasn’t until I started developing my game that I realised I wasn’t used to seeing AI-generated images, and I didn’t realise just how out of place they looked. I’m trying to create a consistent style that looks good and doesn’t look like AI slop. Any advice?

replies.author: ImaginaryProgram142
replies.body:
Sure no problem. I'm working on a Unity 3D project. I'd say my most robust workflow is the one I use for 3D models that uses this stack:

ChatGPT: Sketches, concept art  
Meshy AI: Models, textures (Meshy is probably not longer the best tool anymore)  
Blender: Retopo, cleanup, texture improvements  
Unity: Materials, prefabs, lighting, and gameplay

  
One thing I've been noticing is that there is a very vocal portion of gamers and developers who are strongly opposed to AI. If you use any AI assets or AI assisted workflows, many of them will blacklist you. So with that in mind, I would expect to see some losses on total units shipped, especially at this point in time. You will always get called out for AI slop. That doesn't mean you can't have a commercial success, or make something meaningful for yourself and others.

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: From what I’ve seen, making a 3D game with the help of AI doesn’t usually pose much of a problem, as I don’t think most people will notice it. I think 2D is where the problem lies. I certainly realise it won’t be as successful as a game without AI, but even so, for now I’m happy with the number of wishlists and how it’s turning out. Thanks for your advice!

replies.author: ImaginaryProgram142
replies.body: Best of luck and congrats on the wishlists!

comments.author: EmotionalFan5429
comments.body: There are million of different AI models and you chose most old one... Go to sites like [Fab.ai](http://Fab.ai) and pick other models and LoRAs!

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: I hadn’t used generative AI much until I started working on the visual aspect of the project. From what I could see, Midjourney produced an aesthetically pleasing result, but perhaps I don’t have a particularly trained eye for this sort of thing and it looks a bit rough. I’ll give what you suggested a go! Thanks for the advice!

comments.author: TriggerHydrant
comments.body: I like the right part better and screams less 'AI' to me!

replies.author: Blasckout
replies.body: Thank you for sharing your opinion! I also think that pixel art doesn’t quite give that feeling. Although it might be a bit less aesthetically pleasing.

replies.author: TriggerHydrant
replies.body: Yes! Best wishes with your projects :)

comments.author: EnterpriseGradePizza
comments.body:
Anything generated by AI will look like it's generated by AI. Why does that surprise you? People are rightfully put off by "AI art" because art for all intents and purposes is something that's conveyed from a person to person, whether it be drawn by pencil, oil or digital stylus they are still drawn and there is no middle man like AI that picks and chooses the pixels based off of its back propagation. 

AI cannot convey any emotion, hence will never be a replacement for genuine art used in games.
